:::{#def-eigenvalue}
#### Eigenvalue and eigenvector

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ matrix.
A real number $\eigval$ is an **eigenvalue** of $\matr{A}$
if some real vector $\vecf{v} \neq \vzero$ of length $p$ satisfies

$$
\underbrace{\matr{A}}_{p \times p}\,\underbrace{\vecf{v}}_{p \times 1}
= \eigval\,\underbrace{\vecf{v}}_{p \times 1}
$$

Any such $\vecf{v}$ is an **eigenvector** of $\matr{A}$ for $\eigval$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-eigenvalue}
#### Eigenvectors of a $2 \times 2$ matrix

Let $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

$(1, 1)$ is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue $3$:

$$
\ba
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 1 \\ 1 + 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix-vector multiplication)}
\\
&= 3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(factor out } 3 \text{)}
\ea
$$

$(1, -1)$ is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue $1$:

$$
\ba
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 - 1 \\ 1 - 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix-vector multiplication)}
\\
&= 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(factor out } 1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-eigenvector-multiples}
#### Multiples of an eigenvector

Multiplying by $\matr{A}$ rescales an eigenvector by $\eigval$
and does not change the line it lies on.
Any nonzero multiple $c\,\vecf{v}$ of an eigenvector
is also an eigenvector for the same $\eigval$:

$$
\ba
\matr{A}(c\,\vecf{v})
&= c\,\matr{A}\vecf{v}
&& \text{(move the scalar } c \text{ to the front)}
\\
&= c\,\eigval\vecf{v}
&& \text{(} \vecf{v} \text{ is an eigenvector for } \eigval \text{)}
\\
&= \eigval\,(c\,\vecf{v})
&& \text{(multiplication of numbers is commutative)}
\ea
$$

For example, in @exm-eigenvalue,
$2\,(1, 1) = (2, 2)$ is also an eigenvector for the eigenvalue $3$:

$$
\ba
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \cd 2 + 1 \cd 2 \\ 1 \cd 2 + 2 \cd 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix-vector multiplication)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 4 + 2 \\ 2 + 4 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(add)}
\\
&= 3 \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(factor out } 3 \text{)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-not-eigenvector}
#### A vector that is not an eigenvector

For the same $\matr{A}$,
$(1, 0)$ is not an eigenvector:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix},
$$

and no number $\eigval$ gives $(2, 1) = \eigval\,(1, 0)$,
because the second entries would need $1 = \eigval \cd 0$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-real-eigenvalues}
#### Real and complex eigenvalues

These notes take $\eigval$ and $\vecf{v}$ to be real.
@banerjee2014linear [Chapter 11, Definition 11.1, pp. 312-313]
also allows [complex](algebra.qmd#def-complex-number) eigenvalues and eigenvectors,
because some real matrices, such as a rotation by $90$ degrees,
have no real eigenvalues
[@banerjee2014linear, Chapter 11, Example 11.2, p. 312].

For example,
$\matr{R} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}$
rotates each vector in the plane counterclockwise by $90$ degrees:
$\matr{R}\,(v_1, v_2) = (-v_2, v_1)$.
Suppose $\matr{R}\vecf{v} = \eigval\vecf{v}$ for a real number $\eigval$.
Matching entries gives $-v_2 = \eigval v_1$ and $v_1 = \eigval v_2$.
Substituting the second equation into the first gives
$-v_2 = \eigval^2 v_2$,
so $(1 + \eigval^2)\, v_2 = 0$.
Since $1 + \eigval^2 > 0$, $v_2 = 0$,
and then

$$
\begin{aligned}
v_1 &= \eigval v_2 \\
&= 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

So the only solution is $\vecf{v} = \vzero$,
and $\matr{R}$ has no real eigenvalue.

:::
